Triggers.value: A specific texture associated with the event

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad
try hard not think about the trauma
I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event

Memory.value: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.

vignette: Andreas had been working at the local department store for five years when the fire broke out on a busy Saturday afternoon. He remembered the sound of shattering glass and the feeling of heat radiating from the flames that engulfed the stockroom. The smell of burning plastic and fabric still lingered in his nostrils, transporting him back to that chaotic moment. As he recalled the event, shame washed over him - he had been in charge of monitoring the store's fire safety equipment that day. In the aftermath, Andreas found himself telling others that it wasn't a big deal, that the damage was minimal and everyone got out safely. He even convinced himself that maybe it hadn't happened at all, or perhaps he'd just imagined the whole thing. This coping mechanism, while providing temporary relief, only seemed to heighten his anxiety when confronted with reminders of the fire. People misbehaving in public triggered a visceral response in Andreas - a sense of unease and helplessness would wash over him as he felt like he was reliving that fateful day. Physical proximity to any store or building with similarities to the one where the fire occurred also made him uneasy, as if the trauma could be contagious. One specific texture still haunted Andreas: the feel of melted plastic beneath his fingertips. During the evacuation, he had inadvertently touched a piece of smoldering debris, searing the sensation into his memory. Even now, when handling products with similar textures at work, Andreas's mind would involuntarily flash back to that moment. To cope, Andreas often found himself suppressing thoughts about the fire, pushing them deep down whenever they arose. However, this only led to a build-up of pent-up emotions and physical tension. He began self-harming as a distraction - cutting his arms or legs to momentarily shift focus away from the traumatic memories. When memories of that day did surface, Andreas experienced them with an unsettling vividness, more real than any ordinary memory. Snapshots of those moments still lingered in his mind: the explosion, the panic, and the aftermath. Each recollection was like a photograph - frozen in time, yet perpetually replaying itself. As the months went by, Andreas's avoidance behaviors started taking a toll on his daily life. He stopped attending social gatherings at shopping centers or malls, fearing that he might be confronted with triggers. His relationships began to suffer as well; his wife noticed the change in him and grew increasingly concerned about his distant behavior. What finally brought Andreas to seek help was an incident at work where a customer's careless actions sparked a small fire in one of the store's display cases. The smell of smoke and flames transported him back, and for a moment, he felt like he was reliving that fateful day all over again. This time, however, something snapped - Andreas realized that his avoidance strategies were no longer working, and that the memories and emotions he'd been trying to suppress had become too much to bear. Andreas now hoped that therapy could help him process the trauma, break free from the suffocating grip of shame, and learn healthier ways to cope with the lingering memories. As he sat in the therapist's office, his eyes dropped, and his voice barely above a whisper, Andreas stammered out a simple yet profound request: "I just want to be able to think about that day without feeling like I'm going to break."
